Falafel is a popular Middle Eastern food. It refers to small, round or slightly flattened balls (or sometimes patties) that are deep-fried until crispy on the outside.---

Falafel is made from chickpeas (sometimes fava beans, or a mix of both). The dried chickpeas are soaked in water overnight to soften them, but — importantly — they are never cooked before being ground. This raw, soaked chickpea paste is then blended with fresh herbs like parsley and cilantro, along with garlic, onion, and spices such as cumin and coriander. A small amount of flour or baking soda is often added to hold everything together and make the balls light and slightly airy inside.

The mixture is shaped into golf ball–sized rounds or small patties, and then deep-fried in oil until the outside turns a deep golden-brown or dark brown.
What it looks, feels, and tastes like

From the outside, falafel has a crispy, crunchy crust with a dark brownish colour. On the inside, it is soft, slightly dense, and green-tinged — that green colour comes from all the fresh herbs mixed in.

The taste is savory, earthy, and herby, with the warm depth of cumin and coriander coming through. It is quite filling because chickpeas are protein-rich and starchy.

Falafel is a very versatile food. The most common way to eat it is stuffed inside a pita bread (a soft, round flatbread with a pocket), along with fresh vegetables like tomato, cucumber, and lettuce, pickled vegetables, and sauces — most commonly tahini sauce (made from sesame paste) or hummus (a dip made from chickpeas). This whole combination is often called a "falafel wrap" or "falafel pita."

It is also served:

  • On a plate as a snack or starter, often with dipping sauces on the side
  • As part of a mezze spread — a Middle Eastern-style meal where many small dishes are served together at once
  • Over rice or salad

The word "falafel" can refer to:

  • A single piece: "I dropped a falafel on my shirt."
  • Several pieces or a portion: "She ordered a plate of falafel."
  • The dish as a concept: "Falafel is one of my favourite street foods."

The plural can be either "falafels" or simply "falafel" — both are widely accepted.
Where it comes from and its cultural importance

Falafel is a staple street food across the Middle East, especially in countries like Egypt, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, and Syria. It has been eaten in this region for centuries. Today, it is eaten all over the world and is especially popular as a vegetarian and vegan option, since it contains no meat or animal products.

In many Middle Eastern cities, small falafel shops called falafel stands serve it fresh and hot from the fryer, wrapped quickly in pita, and handed to customers on the go — much like how a fast-food burger works in the West. It is cheap, filling, and deeply beloved.

In short: falafel is a crispy, herb-filled, deep-fried chickpea ball or patty — a classic Middle Eastern street food, eaten in pita bread with vegetables and sauce, and loved worldwide for its bold flavour and satisfying texture.
